2607.19453v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests candle-based ML models on cryptocurrency spot trading. Its forensic audit of a prior holdout—dates influencing architecture, outcome-horizon leakage, missing artifacts—is a concrete protocol failure worth recording. However, it does not directly contradict or refine our gate; it illustrates a failure mode we already guard against (overfitting to validation splits) rather than proposing a new check.
2607.19453v1.protocol_edit: Add to gate documentation: require that outcome-horizon boundaries are purged at train/validation/test splits before any architecture work uses validation results; require that holdout date ranges are locked before any prior-period exploration; require that raw result directories and seed logs are retained for forensic audit. 2607.19453v1.relevance_reason: The paper's core claim—that ML models with high AUC on extrema prediction fail to produce positive returns after costs—is a negative result on a different asset class (crypto spot) with different execution mechanics and cost structures. 2607.19453v1.title: Predictive Extrema, Unprofitable Policies: An AI-Assisted Audit of Candle-Based Binance Spot Timing Models

2607.19497v1.adaptation: Test the paper's analytical framework (Corollaries 4.10, 5.5, and the attribution in Section 7.3) on NQ futures alone. This means: (1) estimating the autocorrelation function and drift of NQ's volatility-normalized returns; (2) computing the predicted Sharpe ratio from equation (5.12); (3) comparing it to realized backtest performance. The claim becomes: 'The closed-form Sharpe ratio formula predicts NQ trend-following performance from its autocorrelation structure,' rather than 'the formula works across a diversified universe of 84 contracts.' The pooled correlation of 0.94 and slope of 0.98 reported in Section 7.3 cannot be replicated; instead, you get one point estimate per filter span.
2607.19497v1.claim: Trend-following systems on volatility-normalized returns are profitable when long-term autocorrelation is positive, and their Sharpe ratio can be predicted in closed form from the autocorrelation function, drift, and kurtosis of the underlying returns.
2607.19497v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's core claim—that trend-following systems profit from autocorrelation in volatility-normalized returns—is testable on NQ futures. However, the paper analyzes a cross-section of 84 liquid futures contracts (equities, bonds, FX, commodities) to validate its closed-form Sharpe ratio formulas. Testing on a single instrument (NQ) reduces the validation from a cross-sectional study to a single time series, fundamentally changing what is being tested.
2607.19497v1.gate_reason: The paper's analytical framework (equations 5.12, 7.3) and its empirical validation protocol (comparing predicted vs. realized Sharpe across filter spans) offer a concrete acceptance criterion for trend-following claims: does the realized performance match the closed-form prediction from autocorrelation? This is a measurable gate on attribution, not on discovery. It also provides a null model—white-noise trend-following should have zero alpha—against which to judge whether observed NQ trend-following alpha is structural or noise.
2607.19497v1.protocol_edit: Add to the gate: for any trend-following hypothesis that passes, compute the autocorrelation function and drift of NQ's volatility-normalized returns, predict the Sharpe ratio from equation (5.12), and record the gap between predicted and realized. Hypotheses whose realized Sharpe significantly exceeds the prediction from autocorrelation alone are candidates for a mechanism beyond trend persistence; those that match the prediction are explained by autocorrelation and do not warrant further investigation as novel edges.
2607.19497v1.relevance_reason: The paper's contribution is a closed-form analytical framework for predicting trend-following Sharpe ratios from autocorrelation structure. Even adapted to NQ alone, this is a model-fitting and performance-attribution exercise with no actionable edge: it explains *why* trend-following works, not *what to trade differently*. A strategy already knows to use trend-following; this paper tells it how to measure whether its trend-following is working as theory predicts, which is a diagnostic, not a signal.
2607.19497v1.title: The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems

2607.20093v1.acts_on: A strategy would not deploy trend, oscillator, volume, or calendar signals on NQ if this paper's refutation holds; it would know to skip those families and focus trials elsewhere.
2607.20093v1.adaptation: Test the five signal families (trend, oscillator, volume, calendar rules) on NQ daily bars using the 384 training sessions available, accepting that (1) the sample is ~13x smaller than the paper's equity sample, (2) candlestick patterns cannot be tested (event-study design requires many occurrences; 384 days may yield too few), (3) the momentum calibration benchmark cannot be replicated (requires cross-sectional diversification across many instruments), and (4) statistical power will be severely degraded, making INCONCLUSIVE verdicts more likely and REFUTED verdicts harder to achieve. The claim tested becomes: 'Do these five retail signal families deliver material edge on NQ futures under the same three-gate framework (statistical, economic, survival), given severe sample-size constraints?'
2607.20093v1.claim: Five widely promoted retail signal families (trend, oscillator, candlestick, volume, calendar) fail to deliver a positive, economically meaningful, net-of-cost, and survivable edge when tested jointly across statistical significance, economic viability after transaction costs, and finite-bankroll survival under leverage.
2607.20093v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests five retail signal families (trend, oscillator, candlestick, volume, calendar) on equities with a momentum benchmark. We have NQ futures tick data with buy/sell volume, which permits testing trend-following and volume-based rules intraday or on daily bars. However, the paper's sample size is 312 months (26 years) of daily cross-sectional equity data across hundreds of stocks. We have only 384 training sessions (daily bars), which is the binding constraint: the paper's statistical gates require sufficient observations to estimate Sharpe-ratio gaps and CAGR gaps with narrow confidence intervals; 384 daily observations is underpowered for the effect sizes the paper targets (Sharpe gap of 0.2+, CAGR gap of 1%+). The momentum calibration benchmark alone uses 312 months × 1,130 stocks; we cannot replicate that cross-sectional structure on one futures contract.
2607.20093v1.gate_reason: The paper's three-gate protocol (statistical, economic, survival) with pre-declared thresholds, multiplicity correction (Benjamini-Yekutieli), equivalence tests, and the distinction between REFUTED, INCONCLUSIVE, and SUPPORTED verdicts directly informs how we should structure and interpret our own gate. Its falsification of four signal families on a similar instrument provides a concrete baseline for the falsified-families list.
2607.20093v1.hypothesis_edit: Add to the next intraday-continuation hypothesis: test whether the signal survives the three-gate framework (statistical significance after Benjamini-Yekutieli correction, economic viability net of transaction costs, finite-bankroll survival under realistic leverage). Use equivalence tests to distinguish refutation from inconclusiveness.
2607.20093v1.protocol_edit: Adopt the three-gate framework: (1) statistical significance after hierarchical Benjamini-Yekutieli correction for multiplicity, (2) economic viability after transaction costs (specify friction model), (3) finite-bankroll survival under leverage. Use equivalence tests to distinguish refutation from inconclusiveness. Add trend, oscillator, volume, and calendar rules to the falsified-families list with the caveat that sample size on NQ is ~13x smaller than the paper's equity sample, so INCONCLUSIVE verdicts are more likely here.
2607.20093v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a three-gate acceptance protocol (statistical edge after multiplicity correction, economic viability after costs, survival under leverage) with concrete thresholds and a falsification framework that directly addresses how we should judge whether a signal works. It tests five signal families we have not yet systematically ruled out on NQ, and its negative results on retail signals establish a falsified-families baseline that prevents wasted trials.
2607.20093v1.speaks_to_deferral: Addresses the genuinely unresolved question of whether simple retail signal families work at all on this instrument, and under what acceptance criteria we should judge them.
2607.20093v1.title: Retail Trader's Ruin: An Anatomy of Popular Signal Failure

We have only 73 holdout sessions (~73 daily bars), which is severely underpowered for the statistical testing (paired Wilcoxon tests, significance stars) the paper relies on.
