2607.26792v1.gate_reason: The paper addresses forecast consistency, not forecast accuracy or trading performance. It does not propose a null construction, a multiple-testing correction, an acceptance protocol, or evidence about overfitting decay. Its contribution is a mathematical constraint solver, not a change to how we evaluate whether a result generalizes or whether a hypothesis is worth trading.
2607.26792v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a post-hoc reconciliation method for probabilistic OHLC forecasts. Even after removing the forecasting apparatus (which we cannot run), what remains is a constraint-satisfaction procedure with no actionable edge: it enforces logical consistency in forecasts but does not claim or test whether consistent forecasts trade profitably. A strategy cannot act on 'forecasts are now self-consistent'; it can only act on 'these forecasts predict returns.' The paper does not address the latter.
2607.26792v1.title: Crossing-Free Probabilistic K-Line Forecasts Without Retraining

2607.27063v1.claim: Local herding and delayed information diffusion jointly generate momentum and reversal in equity markets, measurable via CSAD and LSV indicators on a cross-section of stocks.
2607.27063v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires cross-sectional equity data (China's A-share market with multiple stocks to measure CSAD and LSV herding indicators) and agent-based simulation validation. We have only one futures instrument (NQ) with no cross-section, no equity constituents, and no ability to compute dispersion-based or institutional-trade herding measures across a universe of stocks.
2607.27063v1.title: Herding, Momentum, and Reversal in China's A-Share Market: An Agent-Based Network Model with Information Diffusion

2607.27070v1.claim: Early-warning signals of critical transitions in leveraged futures crashes are event-heterogeneous; no single state variable (price, leverage, or order flow) carries a reproducible critical-slowing-down signature across crashes, except for a weak population-level compression in taker order-flow variance.
2607.27070v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies seven discrete liquidation cascade events in crypto perpetual futures using minute-level price and 5-minute leverage/order-flow data from Binance. We have only 384 training sessions (daily bars) of NQ futures, yielding 384 observations total—far too few to replicate the paper's multi-event comparative analysis. The paper's central claim requires studying multiple distinct crash events with sufficient pre-crash windows to detect early-warning signals; a single instrument with 384 daily sessions cannot support this event-comparative methodology.
2607.27070v1.title: Where does the criticality live? Early-warning signals are event-heterogeneous across seven crypto-perpetual liquidation cascades

2607.27099v1.claim: Rainfall arrivals follow critical Hawkes processes with heavy-tailed kernels, and aggregated rainfall converges to a rough fractional process with Hurst exponent between 0.01 and 0.1.
2607.27099v1.feasibility_reason: This paper models rainfall dynamics using Hawkes processes, Hurst exponents, and scaling laws across multiple time scales from minutes to centuries. It requires high-frequency rainfall data (minute-scale over years) and low-frequency data (annual observations spanning centuries to millennia). We have only NQ futures tick data with 384 daily sessions (~1.5 years), which is neither rainfall data nor sufficient temporal span for the paper's core claims about long-memory scaling and Hurst exponent estimation.
2607.27099v1.title: Rainfall is rough

2607.27188v1.claim: Learned operators (DeepONet, FNO, transformers) can recover latent risk-neutral densities from sparse, irregular option quotes more accurately on tail functionals and under model misspecification than classical parametric mixtures, though no universal winner exists across all metrics and specifications.
2607.27188v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim concerns recovery of risk-neutral densities from option quotes using inverse learning. We have no options data, no quotes, no bid/ask, no implied volatility surface, and no cross-sectional structure. The paper requires irregular option observations across strikes and maturities; we have only one futures instrument with tick-level trade data.
2607.27188v1.title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes

2607.27461v1.claim: A dynamic portfolio built from three fixed-size matrices (return-correlation distance, return-rank Markov chain, volatility-rank Markov chain) estimated from S&P 500 stock prices and volumes beats the market on an out-of-sample basis with a Sharpe ratio above 1.0.
2607.27461v1.feasibility_reason: The paper requires a cross-section of 500 S&P 500 stocks to build correlation matrices, distance matrices, and rank-based Markov chains across many names. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-sectional analysis impossible. The core claim—that three matrices (correlation distance, return-rank transitions, volatility-rank transitions) built from a universe of stocks can beat the market—is fundamentally a cross-sectional portfolio optimization problem.
2607.27461v1.title: Are Three Matrices All You Need To Beat the Market? Observable Matrix Dynamics for Portfolio Optimization

2607.27485v1.claim: Critical mineral ETFs with higher ESG scores act as net transmitters of volatility shocks within a macro-financial network that includes energy, carbon emissions, market sentiment, and infrastructure variables, with structural shifts during COVID-19.
2607.27485v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies dynamic connectedness and volatility spillovers across seven critical mineral ETFs and four macro variables (WTI, VIX, carbon futures, infrastructure ETF) using TVP-VAR on daily data from May 2013–May 2023. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), no cross-sectional data, no ETF prices, no carbon futures, and no ability to construct the seven mineral portfolios or macro variables the paper requires. The claim fundamentally depends on a multi-asset network analysis that cannot be replicated on a single futures contract.
2607.27485v1.title: Energy Market and Carbon Emission Spillovers in Critical Minerals Investment: A Dynamic Connectedness Approach

2607.27853v2.claim: A specialized financial research harness with layered tools and point-in-time access control improves LLM agent performance on analyst-style financial deep research tasks compared to generic search scaffolds.
2607.27853v2.feasibility_reason: This paper is about evaluating LLM-based research agents on financial deep-research tasks using a benchmark of 400 questions with rubric-based scoring. It requires a corpus of financial documents, a retrieval system, LLM judges, and multi-turn agent trajectories—none of which exist in our single-instrument futures data. The paper's central claim concerns agent performance on analyst-style research synthesis, which is entirely orthogonal to intraday or daily trading on NQ futures.
2607.27853v2.title: FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework

2607.28127v1.claim: Market-aligned reinforcement learning can train an LLM to extract sentiment signals from financial news articles that outperform static supervised sentiment models when deployed in a long-short equity portfolio.
2607.28127v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires financial news articles paired with their realized market outcomes to train a sentiment-analysis LLM via reinforcement learning. We have only tick-level NQ futures data with no news feed, no fundamental data, and no cross-sectional equity universe. The paper tests on S&P 500 stocks with news from 2015–2021; our instrument is a single futures contract with no text data whatsoever.
2607.28127v1.title: FinSMART: Financial Sentiment Analysis for Algorithmic Trading through Market-Aligned Reinforcement Learning

2607.28230v2.claim: In a finite-horizon multiplicative process with an absorbing lower boundary and fixed fractional exposure, optimal exposure is compressed below the Kelly fraction near the boundary and recovers toward it as distance increases, with this compression appearing as elevated risk aversion when interpreted through a no-boundary CRRA benchmark.
2607.28230v2.feasibility_reason: This paper is a theoretical study of optimal exposure selection in a finite-horizon multiplicative process with an absorbing boundary. It contains no empirical component, no data analysis, and no testable predictions about market behavior. The central claim—that boundary-induced geometry generates state-dependent risk-averse-looking behavior without preference heterogeneity—is a mathematical result about an abstract binary gamble, not a claim about futures price dynamics or trading strategy performance.
2607.28230v2.title: Boundary-Induced Apparent Risk Aversion in Nonergodic Multiplicative Growth

2607.28294v1.claim: Fixed-count bootstrap inference remains valid for ACD model parameters even when durations have infinite mean (κ < 1), reproducing the conditional Gaussian component of the mixed-normal limiting distribution.
2607.28294v1.feasibility_reason: The paper develops bootstrap inference theory for autoregressive conditional duration (ACD) models, which require irregularly-spaced event data with inter-arrival times as the core object. Our data are regularly-spaced trades on a single futures contract with tick-level resolution. While we can compute durations between trades, the paper's theoretical contributions concern inference on duration model parameters (persistence, conditional mean structure) estimated from a fixed calendar span with random event counts. Testing this requires either (1) a duration model fitted to our trade data and inference on its parameters, or (2) validation that the bootstrap theory applies to our specific duration process. Neither is the paper's claim. The paper is about bootstrap methodology for duration models, not about whether duration models work on futures data.
2607.28294v1.title: Bootstrap inference in autoregressive duration models

2607.28323v1.claim: Optimal execution with passive limit orders can be modeled by combining exponentially-decaying fill probabilities with distance from midprice and linear order-flow-imbalance price impact, yielding a tractable optimal liquidation problem where traders control quote aggressiveness.
2607.28323v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires order-book microstructure data (limit-order placements, cancellations, queue positions, and multi-level depth) to estimate fill intensities and MLOFI price-impact coefficients. We have only tick-level trade data with aggressor side, no order-book events, no quotes, and no depth. The paper explicitly calibrates on NASDAQ LOBSTER data (full order-book reconstruction) and LSEG FX L2 quotes; neither is available here.
2607.28323v1.title: Optimal Execution with Passive Market Impact

2607.28410v1.claim: Large language models can reduce execution costs in parent-order execution by decomposing the problem into long-horizon planning and short-horizon execution, outperforming TWAP and traditional baselines by 0.65 basis points.
2607.28410v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests parent-order execution on Chinese stock exchange data with bid/ask quotes and intraday volume patterns. We have only NQ futures tick data with no quotes, no order book depth, and no intraday volume distribution. More critically, parent-order execution is a cross-sectional problem requiring multiple stocks or instruments to generate realistic parent orders and test execution strategies; a single futures contract cannot generate the heterogeneous parent-order characteristics (different stocks, volatilities, liquidity profiles) that the paper's evaluation depends on.
2607.28410v1.title: Can Large Language Models Execute Parent Orders?

2607.28577v1.claim: A deployment policy that compares a retrained model candidate against a continuously maintained incumbent on paired forward labels, promoting only after a fixed NLL advantage, improves probabilistic forecasts while reducing model-state turnover relative to calendar replacement and automatic promotion.
2607.28577v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim concerns a model deployment policy (Shadow Before Swap) evaluated on crypto perpetual futures with order-book depth data. We lack order-book depth entirely—the paper uses 60 snapshots of 40-band depth features per prediction, which is not constructible from our tick-level trade data. Additionally, the claim requires testing on multiple underlyings (BTC, ETH, BNB, XRP, SOL, DOGE, ADA, BCH) across two contract types; we have only one instrument (NQ futures).
2607.28577v1.title: Train Often, Deploy Selectively: Forward-Gated Model Replacement in Crypto Markets

2607.28847v1.claim: Rejected loan applicants from protected demographic groups face systematically higher effort (weighted cost of feature changes) to reach approval than privileged groups, even when the model satisfies standard predictive-parity fairness criteria, and this masked inequality can be mitigated by embedding effort-parity constraints into model training.
2607.28847v1.feasibility_reason: This paper studies algorithmic fairness in mortgage credit scoring using a cross-sectional dataset of ~500k loan originations with demographic and credit attributes. It requires: (1) a cross-section of applicants with heterogeneous features (income, debt ratios, credit scores, loan amounts, demographics) to measure effort disparities across groups; (2) a classifier trained on default outcomes to define an approval boundary; (3) causal structure learning over feature relationships. We have only one futures instrument with tick-level trade data, no applicant-level features, no demographics, no cross-section of decision subjects, and no default outcomes or credit risk labels.
2607.28847v1.title: Effort-Centric Fairness in Lending Decisions

2607.29220v1.claim: A decoupled diffusion-based probabilistic forecasting framework with surface-aware attention refinement can forecast implied volatility surfaces while satisfying static no-arbitrage constraints.
2607.29220v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires options data with implied volatility surfaces across strikes and maturities. We have only NQ futures tick data with no options, no quotes, no order book, and no cross-sectional dimension. Implied volatility surfaces cannot be constructed from a single futures instrument.
2607.29220v1.title: Decoupled Probabilistic Forecasting and Arbitrage-Aware Refinement of Implied Volatility Surfaces

2608.00127v1.adaptation: Construct daily P&L from NQ tick data. Estimate process Sharpe, volatility, skewness, kurtosis, and autocorrelation on the training set. Compare observed maximum drawdown, maximum loss, final negative time, and longest recovery time on the validation and holdout sets against the paper's predicted quantiles for the estimated Sharpe and archetype. Accept that parameter estimates will be noisy and that the test is underpowered; report uncertainty bands. Do not attempt to estimate Hurst exponent reliably—treat Section 5 (fractional Brownian motion) as infeasible on this sample size.
2608.00127v1.claim: For a given Sharpe ratio and return distribution (skewness, kurtosis, autocorrelation), the quantiles of maximum drawdown, maximum loss, time under water, and recovery time follow the Monte-Carlo distributions predicted by the paper's framework, with depth-type measures insensitive to horizon and time-type measures growing with it.
2608.00127v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim—that drawdown risk depends on Sharpe ratio, return distribution shape, and long memory—can be tested on NQ futures returns. However, the paper is a theoretical/simulation study with no empirical validation on real strategy returns. Testing requires: (1) constructing daily P&L from NQ trades, (2) estimating its Sharpe, skewness, kurtosis, autocorrelation, and Hurst exponent, and (3) comparing observed drawdown quantiles to the paper's predicted tables. The binding constraint is sample size: 384 training sessions = 384 daily observations, which is barely sufficient to estimate a Sharpe ratio reliably (Lo standard error ~0.16 for 3 years) and too small to estimate higher moments, GARCH parameters, or Hurst exponent with precision. The paper's own Section 4.2 notes that 'data available are rarely sufficient to identify richer specifications without overfitting,' and the paper itself uses 3-year (750-day) simulations. Our 384 observations fall short.
2608.00127v1.gate_reason: The paper's Monte-Carlo framework and lookup tables could serve as a calibration check on our acceptance protocol: we could compare observed drawdown quantiles against the paper's predictions given estimated Sharpe, skewness, kurtosis, and autocorrelation, and flag strategies whose drawdown behavior deviates from the model as either overfitted or genuinely anomalous.
2608.00127v1.protocol_edit: Add a post-acceptance validation step: for each accepted strategy, estimate its return distribution (Sharpe, volatility, skewness, kurtosis, autocorrelation) on the training set, compute the paper's predicted quantiles for maximum drawdown and recovery time, and report whether observed drawdowns on validation and holdout sets fall within the 90% prediction band. Strategies whose drawdowns are systematically deeper than predicted may indicate overfitting or regime dependence not captured by the marginal distribution.
2608.00127v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a framework for *evaluating* drawdown risk given a strategy's statistical properties, not a mechanism to trade on or a condition under which an edge appears. It is a measurement tool and a risk model, not an actionable claim.
2608.00127v1.title: Drawdown Risk Beyond Brownian Motion: A Monte-Carlo Framework, Non-Gaussian Extensions, and Long Memory

2608.00616v2.claim: A latent flow-matching generative model can produce arbitrage-free implied volatility surfaces that balance distributional fidelity with financial consistency better than diffusion and GAN baselines.
2608.00616v2.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires implied volatility surfaces from equity options (SPX). We have only NQ futures tick data with no options market, no quotes, no bid/ask, and no way to derive or observe implied volatility surfaces. The entire generative framework depends on option-derived data that does not exist in our instrument.
2608.00616v2.title: Latent Flow Matching for Arbitrage-Aware Implied Volatility Surface Generation

2608.00631v1.claim: A physically backed margin layer over binary event outcome tokens can separate leverage maturity from claim maturity, extinguish debt before oracle finality through a robust ex-ante hard-flat sale, and preserve the lender's principal from terminal payout and dispute-duration risk.
2608.00631v1.feasibility_reason: This paper specifies a margin-lending mechanism for binary event prediction markets with leveraged outcome-token positions. It requires: (1) a second instrument (outcome tokens from a binary event market with oracle finality and redemption), (2) order-book depth and liquidity data from that market, (3) settlement and finality timing data, (4) oracle proposal and challenge data, and (5) multi-day or multi-week holding periods to observe leverage maturity, claim maturity, and redemption. We have only one futures contract with tick-level data, no event tokens, no oracle system, and 384 daily sessions. The paper's central claim—that a margin layer can extinguish debt before oracle finality while preserving residual spot exposure—cannot be tested on NQ futures.
2608.00631v1.title: Axient: Debt-Free Finality for Leveraged Binary Event Markets

2608.00647v1.claim: An on-chain credit protocol for leveraged event positions can allocate losses deterministically across traders, Senior LPs, LBPs, and reserves while maintaining withdrawal honesty and preventing contagion, and endogenous capital-provider participation, market-maker delivery, and liquidator entry will reduce but not eliminate Senior loss under stress.
2608.00647v1.feasibility_reason: This paper designs an on-chain credit protocol for leveraged event markets using agent-based modeling with synthetic behavioral rules and hypothetical capital-market dynamics. It requires multi-agent heterogeneous behavior (Senior LPs, LBPs, traders, market makers, liquidators), cross-sectional capital-supply responses, withdrawal runs, and common-factor contagion—none of which can be observed or tested on a single futures instrument with 384 training sessions. The paper's central claim concerns protocol design and endogenous capital-market equilibrium, not intraday price patterns or order-flow effects.
2608.00647v1.title: Axient: On-Chain Credit and Loss Allocation for Leveraged Event Markets: A Venue-Agnostic Protocol for Traders, Credit Providers, Market Makers, and Liquidation Backstops

2608.00761v1.claim: AI-derived measures of economic fundamental strength, constructed from economic data releases, can predict next-month currency returns in a cross-sectional strategy that goes long strong currencies and short weak currencies, with a Sharpe ratio exceeding 0.7 per annum.
2608.00761v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests a cross-sectional currency strategy across 9 G-10 currency pairs, requiring multiple instruments and their exchange rates. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-sectional ranking and long/short positioning across currencies impossible. Additionally, the paper's core claim requires economic calendar data (544 unique indicators: GDP, employment, inflation, central bank decisions) which we do not have.
2608.00761v1.title: AI and Exchange Rate Predictability

2608.00858v2.claim: Machine learning models trained on proprietary HFT identifiers can map public intraday variables to separate liquidity-supplying from liquidity-demanding HFT activity, and this separation reveals that supply-side HFT lowers spreads and improves information acquisition while demand-side HFT does the opposite.
2608.00858v2.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires measuring HFT activity and its effects on market quality across thousands of stocks over 14 years. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), which provides a single cross-section with no variation across securities. The paper's entire methodology—training ML models on 120 stocks' HFT identifiers, then applying to 8,314 U.S. stocks—is impossible on a single futures contract. Additionally, the paper studies information acquisition around earnings announcements, bid-ask spreads, and informed trading intensity, none of which are testable on futures data.
2608.00858v2.title: Data-Driven Measures of High-Frequency Trading

2608.00885v1.acts_on: A strategy would enter a symmetric band around an estimated latent efficient price (via Hasbrouck or Kalman filtering), with half-width θ* derived from the stationary variance of the gap and the spread, rather than using raw price continuation or flow features.
2608.00885v1.adaptation: Test on intraday NQ futures (1-minute or 5-minute bars constructible from ticks). Estimate the efficient price via Hasbrouck decomposition or Kalman filtering on the observed mid and spread (both available from our data). Implement the band strategy using the filtered gap estimate rather than the true latent gap. This tests whether the band's closed-form formula remains profitable under realistic filtering error, not the paper's full-information benchmark. The claim becomes: 'mean-reversion bands optimized for a latent gap remain profitable when the gap is estimated from quotes and trades.'
2608.00885v1.claim: A symmetric no-churn trading band with half-width θ* solving θ*(θ*−φ)=s_G² maximizes long-run profit rate on mean-reverting microstructure noise, earning R*=αs_G√(2/π)e^(−θ*²/2s_G²) net of bid-ask spread.
2608.00885v1.feasibility_first_pass_reason: The paper requires order book depth, bid-ask quotes, and message-level data to observe the latent efficient price, mid-price jumps, and order flow dynamics that drive mean reversion. We have only trade ticks with aggressor side, no quotes or book state.
2608.00885v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's core claim—optimal mean-reversion trading via symmetric bands on a latent gap—is testable on NQ futures tick data. However, the paper assumes the efficient price is observable (Section 2.1, Definition 2.1), which is latent in reality. The adaptation requires filtering the gap from observed mid and spread, reducing the claim from full-information to filtered-information trading. Additionally, the paper's theoretical optimum is derived for a surrogate Gaussian diffusion; testing on the actual jump process introduces a timing error the paper leaves heuristic (Section 3, error (c)).
2608.00885v1.gate_reason: The paper offers no acceptance protocol, null construction, multiple-testing correction, or measurement of out-of-sample decay. It does not contradict or refine the gate's thresholds (t ≥ 2.0, ≥ 30 trades per fold, positive net after friction, stability across years). A negative result on mean-reversion bands would be gate-relevant; a theoretical optimum is not.
2608.00885v1.hypothesis_edit: Add to intraday-continuation: condition on the estimated gap between observed mid and latent efficient price (via Hasbrouck decomposition or Kalman filter); test whether mean-reversion bands with θ* = √(s_G² + φ·s_G) outperform raw continuation. Name the filtering method and its error bound as part of the hypothesis.
2608.00885v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a closed-form band strategy for mean-reversion trading that is separable from its theoretical apparatus and testable on our data via the Stage 1 adaptation (Hasbrouck/Kalman filtering of the latent gap, then band entry/exit). The mechanism — mean reversion of microstructure noise around an efficient price — is actionable and would change how we condition on price state. However, it speaks to intraday-continuation, which has been rejected repeatedly, and the paper does not name a condition under which mean reversion appears or fails that would distinguish this from prior attempts.
2608.00885v1.speaks_to_deferral: Addresses intraday-continuation (a closed question, rejected repeatedly) by proposing a specific mechanism (microstructure mean reversion) and a specific state (latent gap) rather than a new condition under which continuation appears or fails.
2608.00885v1.title: Optimal Trading of Microstructure Mean Reversion

2608.00911v1.claim: Adaptive Refinement Bayesian Optimization (ARBO-DART) efficiently co-optimizes battery energy storage dispatch across day-ahead and real-time electricity markets by adaptively refining the day-ahead commitment profile based on real-time recourse value.
2608.00911v1.feasibility_reason: This paper optimizes battery storage dispatch across day-ahead and real-time electricity markets using Bayesian optimization. We have only one futures instrument (NQ) with no electricity market data, no battery state-of-charge dynamics, no day-ahead vs real-time price structure, and no ability to model the two-settlement electricity market framework that is central to the paper's claim.
2608.00911v1.title: Battery Storage Co-Optimization in Day-Ahead and Real-Time Markets with Bayesian Optimization

2608.00988v1.claim: The square-root price-impact law (α=0.5) is necessary and sufficient for diffusive price dynamics even when market-order flow exhibits long-range correlations due to institutional order splitting.
2608.00988v1.feasibility_reason: The paper is a theoretical microstructure model testing whether the square-root price-impact law resolves the diffusive price-dynamics paradox under long-range correlated order flow. It requires order-level data with trader identities, metaorder sizes, and order-splitting sequences to construct the Lillo-Mike-Farmer model and measure order-flow autocorrelation. We have only tick-level aggressor side (buy/sell), not order-level data, trader IDs, or metaorder boundaries.
2608.00988v1.title: Exactly solvable model for the diffusive price-dynamics paradox under long-range correlated market-order flow

2608.02311v2.claim: Financial institutions lack operational governance frameworks for agentic AI systems (88% gap), and a four-layer governance architecture (Policy, Engineering, Composition, Systemic) grounded in reward-function review, policy-drift monitoring, vendor-dependency controls, and crowding disclosure is necessary and sufficient to address failure modes that deterministic governance frameworks cannot catch.
2608.02311v2.feasibility_reason: This paper is a governance and risk-management framework for agentic AI systems in finance. It requires cross-sectional data (multiple institutions, multiple strategies, survey evidence, regulatory filings, case studies across different domains: trading, fraud, payments, customer service) and institutional-level analysis. Our data is a single futures instrument with 384 training sessions—far too small and narrow to test any of the paper's central claims about governance gaps, policy drift detection, compositional risk, or systemic crowding.
2608.02311v2.title: AI Governance for Institutional Readiness in Finance

2608.02475v1.claim: The DeTEcT framework can quantify the impact of endogenous policy events (BIPs) on wealth distribution dynamics in token economies by comparing interaction rates before and after events, with significance assessed against contextual baselines.
2608.02475v1.feasibility_reason: This paper models token economy wealth distribution dynamics using agent-based simulation (DeTEcT framework) applied to Bitcoin's Gini-like wealth buckets. It requires daily wealth distribution data across multiple wealth brackets over years, plus event timestamps (BIPs). We have only intraday NQ futures tick data with no wealth distribution, no cross-sectional agent categories, and no ability to construct the required state variables.
2608.02475v1.title: Methodology for Modelling Token Economies and Performing Event Impact Analysis with DeTEcT

2608.02778v1.claim: Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs can reduce the RMSE of coarse-mesh PDE solutions for multi-asset and barrier option pricing by a factor of 4–12 using minimal high-fidelity training data.
2608.02778v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim is about accelerating PDE-based option pricing via neural network correction of numerical solvers. This requires (1) options data with implied volatility or market prices to validate pricing accuracy, (2) multi-asset or barrier option structures, and (3) the ability to solve Black-Scholes and Heston PDEs as benchmarks. We have only single-instrument NQ futures tick data with no options chain, no volatility surface, no option prices, and no way to construct or validate option pricing models.
2608.02778v1.title: Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs for Efficient Options Pricing Models

2608.02828v2.claim: Proper-score observation-driven filters separate the roles of predictive density and updating criterion, with relative performance depending on the target and disturbance, as demonstrated through volatility forecasting on international equity indices.
2608.02828v2.feasibility_reason: This paper develops theoretical properties of observation-driven filters using proper scoring rules, with applications to volatility forecasting on equity indices. It requires cross-sectional equity data (12 international markets) and daily observations to estimate and compare filtering models. We have only one futures instrument with 384 training sessions, making cross-sectional comparisons and the empirical validation of the paper's claims impossible.
2608.02828v2.title: Proper-score observation-driven filters: local geometry, estimation, and continuous-time limits

2608.02917v1.claim: A geometric mean market maker with a multi-asset fee structure can outperform traditional target-weighted mutual funds and ETFs in both tracking error and returns when rebalanced by arbitrage.
2608.02917v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires testing a multi-asset portfolio rebalancing strategy (60/40 equity/bond, equal-weighted sectors, equal-weighted DJIA) against real mutual funds and ETFs. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-asset portfolio construction and mandate tracking impossible. The paper's empirical validation depends on comparing tracked indices and multiple asset classes; neither is available.
2608.02917v1.title: Mandate without Managers: Automated Market Makers as Verifiable Portfolio Products

2608.03088v1.adaptation: Test the LAE specification test on intraday NQ futures (1-minute or 5-minute bars to increase observations per session) rather than daily data. Alternatively, use the 384 daily sessions but acknowledge this severely limits power and may not replicate the paper's Monte Carlo findings, which assume much larger samples. The test itself is model-agnostic and works on any univariate ergodic Markov process.
2608.03088v1.claim: A density-based goodness-of-fit test for ergodic Markov processes can detect departures from a parametric null hypothesis by comparing the theoretical stationary density to a consistent density estimator, with nontrivial power against local alternatives and no smoothing parameter selection required.
2608.03088v1.feasibility_first_pass_reason: This is a theoretical statistics paper on goodness-of-fit testing methodology for Markov processes. It does not propose a trading strategy, market microstructure hypothesis, or price prediction model testable on market data. The paper's contribution is methodological (a new statistical test), not empirical.
2608.03088v1.feasibility_reason: The paper proposes a goodness-of-fit test for ergodic Markov processes based on comparing stationary densities. This is testable on NQ futures as a univariate Markov process, but the binding constraint is sample size: the paper's theory and examples use interest rate models and business cycle data with hundreds or thousands of observations, while we have only 384 training sessions for daily bars.
2608.03088v1.gate_reason: A specification test for ergodic Markov processes could inform how we evaluate whether a fitted model (e.g., a continuation or absorption hypothesis) is well-specified, and whether departures from the null matter for trading. It bears on the accounting and acceptance protocol, not on a new campaign.
2608.03088v1.protocol_edit: Add a specification check to the gate: after fitting a Markov model to intraday state transitions, test whether the empirical stationary density matches the model's theoretical density using LAE or similar. Reject models that fail this test before evaluating trading performance, to avoid building strategies on mis-specified dynamics.
2608.03088v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a statistical test for model specification, not a trading mechanism or feature. Even adapted to intraday bars, it answers 'does this model fit?' not 'what should the strategy do differently?' No actionable edge survives removal of the apparatus.
2608.03088v1.title: A New Approach to Goodness of Fit for Ergodic Markov Processes

2608.03616v1.claim: Liquidation cascades are first-order transitions (not critical) with subcritical branching ratios measurable in flight from on-chain fill logs, whose severity is set by liquidity withdrawal rather than leverage divergence.
2608.03616v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies crypto-perpetual liquidation cascades using cross-asset correlation structure, branching ratios, and on-chain fill logs from multiple venues (Binance, Hyperliquid). We have only one futures instrument (NQ), no cross-sectional data, no liquidation mechanics, no multi-venue data, and no fill-level attribution. The core claim—measuring branching ratios and first-order transition signatures in a cascade—requires the multi-asset, multi-venue infrastructure that does not exist in our data.
2608.03616v1.title: Measuring the engine of a liquidation cascade: subcritical branching inside a first-order transition

2608.04373v3.claim: Persistent pseudonymous wallet addresses that reveal trader identity carry short-horizon price information that anonymous order-book data leave unmeasured, as evidenced by wallet-level markout persistence predicting one-second returns.
2608.04373v3.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires persistent wallet identity tracking across time to measure trader informativeness and predict returns. Our data is a single anonymous futures instrument with no wallet addresses, trader identifiers, or any mechanism to link orders across time to specific accounts. The core finding—that wallet-level markout persistence predicts returns—cannot be tested without the ability to identify and track individual traders.
2608.04373v3.title: Public Trader Identity: Adverse Selection and Return Predictability

2608.04832v1.claim: Policies trained under stationary ambiguity (where parameter uncertainty does not systematically decay over time) maintain robustness to latent regime shifts, whereas policies trained under vanishing ambiguity (static randomization) specialize to observed regimes and fail when parameters change.
2608.04832v1.feasibility_first_pass_reason: The paper's core claim—that policies trained under stationary ambiguity remain robust to latent regime shifts—can be tested on NQ futures hedging or directional control. The binding constraint is that we have only 384 train sessions (daily bars), which is tight for deep RL but sufficient for a proof-of-concept. The paper's hedging experiments are on derivatives; we can substitute a directional or volatility-targeting strategy on NQ futures instead.
2608.04832v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires testing hedging policies on simulated price paths with latent volatility regimes that shift over time. We have only one instrument (NQ futures) with 384 training sessions, making it impossible to construct the multi-asset hedging problems (straddles, worst-of calls, risk reversals on different underlyings) or to generate the controlled regime-shift scenarios the paper uses to evaluate 'continual robustness.' The paper's core contribution—that stationary ambiguity preserves robustness to latent parameter shifts—cannot be isolated on a single futures contract.
2608.04832v1.gate_reason: The paper's core contribution—that stationary ambiguity preserves robustness while decaying ambiguity causes specialization—is a claim about out-of-sample decay and what predicts it. This bears on how we measure and interpret robustness across regimes. However, the mechanism (RL policy learning under different simulator assumptions) is not directly comparable to our acceptance protocol, which is walk-forward validation on fixed feature sets.
2608.04832v1.protocol_edit: The paper suggests measuring whether a policy trained on one regime distribution remains robust when latent parameters shift. This could inform a gate check: does a strategy's performance degrade predictably when we test it on sessions with different volatility regimes or microstructure parameters? Add a regime-shift robustness measurement to the holdout evaluation, separate from walk-forward stability.
2608.04832v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a training procedure for RL policies in simulation, but the project has already falsified sequence models and deep networks at current sample size, and explicitly defers reinforcement learning pending resolution of reward-shaping questions. The adapted claim requires training a policy end-to-end, which is a project (machinery we do not have calibrated), not a campaign actionable on Tuesday.
2608.04832v1.speaks_to_deferral: auction-market-features (defers RL and deep networks), but the deferral is structural, not a question to resolve first.
2608.04832v1.title: Robust Control under Stationary Ambiguity

2608.05373v1.claim: A pump-and-crash manipulation signature visible in option Delta velocity can be detected at minute resolution with high recall on enforcement-labeled dates, and this signature transfers across markets and instrument types.
2608.05373v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires options market data (option prices, implied volatility, Delta, Greeks) and enforcement-labeled manipulation dates from two jurisdictions (Indian BANKNIFTY index options and U.S. equities from SEC v. Patel). We have only NQ futures tick data with no options chain, no Greeks, and no enforcement labels. The signature detection method is fundamentally built on option-state dynamics that do not exist in our data.
2608.05373v1.title: Velocity- and Regime-Aware Detection of Intraday Options Market Manipulation, with Explainable Attribution

2608.05755v2.claim: Learnable sector embeddings in LSTM networks improve directional return prediction by capturing industry momentum, a cross-sectional phenomenon requiring multiple stocks across different sectors.
2608.05755v2.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a cross-section of S&P 500 stocks (500 constituents) to test sector embeddings and industry momentum effects. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-sectional heterogeneity and sector-level analysis impossible. The claim fundamentally depends on multiple assets with sector classifications.
2608.05755v2.title: Cross-Sectional Heterogeneity in LSTM Networks for Financial Time Series

2608.06048v1.claim: Given name frequency distributions in the USA and France follow Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation, producing stable Lorenz and Pareto curves with Gini coefficients between 0.85–0.95 over 100+ years.
2608.06048v1.feasibility_reason: This paper analyzes statistical distributions of baby names from government databases using Lorenz curves, Pareto distributions, and Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization theory. It requires cross-sectional demographic data (name frequencies across populations over time), not financial time series. The claim is entirely about social/demographic statistics and has no connection to trading, market microstructure, or price dynamics.
2608.06048v1.title: Thermodynamic statistics of given names in USA and France

2608.06618v1.claim: Joint factor-graph learning that redefines graph locality through factor exposures rather than co-movement produces portfolios that outperform correlation-based allocation across market regimes.
2608.06618v1.feasibility_reason: The paper requires a cross-section of 300 equities (S&P 500, Nikkei 225, STOXX 600 constituents) to learn joint factor-graph representations and test portfolio diversification. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-sectional analysis impossible. Additionally, the claim depends on comparing graph-based clustering against economic sectors (GICS), which requires multiple assets with sector labels—not applicable to a single futures contract.
2608.06618v1.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification

2608.07690v1.claim: Order imbalance in customer arrivals is absorbed exactly by a translation of the market maker's skew, a widening of quotes, and a multiplication of carrying cost, with the adjustment determined by the observable market width and the log-odds of arrival direction.
2608.07690v1.feasibility_reason: The paper is a theoretical market-making model for OTC dealer markets with sealed-bid auctions. It requires order-flow direction (buy/sell imbalance), competing quotes, and win rates—none of which exist in our data. NQ futures are continuous electronic limit-order markets, not OTC request-for-quote mechanisms, and we have no competing dealer quotes or win/loss outcomes on submitted bids.
2608.07690v1.title: On a Simple Relationship Between Order Imbalance, Skew and Width in Over-The-Counter Trading

2608.07709v1.claim: A Poisson-embedded marked Hawkes order-flow model with ordinary arrivals and rare marked arrivals converges in distribution to the rough Hawkes–Heston stochastic volatility model under near-critical scaling.
2608.07709v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is a pure mathematical finance theory paper proving convergence of a microscopic marked Hawkes order-flow model to a rough Hawkes–Heston stochastic volatility limit. It requires order-level data (marked Hawkes point processes with event classifications, marks, and intensities) and makes no empirical claims testable on price/volume data alone. The paper contains no backtests, no strategy, no performance metrics on real data—only convergence proofs and numerical illustrations of the theoretical limit.
2608.07709v1.title: Microstructural Foundation for the Rough Hawkes--Heston Model

2608.08625v1.claim: Partial retention of hidden excess clipped by daily price limits generates same-sign next-day mean returns and persistence probabilities that scale with band width.
2608.08625v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires daily price-limit circuit breaker events as the triggering mechanism. NQ futures have no daily price limits (they trade continuously with only intraday circuit breakers that do not clip returns). Without limit-close events, the core latent-state model cannot be tested.
2608.08625v1.title: Retained hidden excess generates memory in price-limited markets

2608.08825v1.claim: Hybrid neural-classical correction (combining frozen TimesFM with attention or bilinear neural modules plus Random Forest residual learning) achieves superior intraday return prediction on equities compared to frozen foundation models alone, with classical residual learning providing the largest single-component contribution.
2608.08825v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies intraday return prediction on 10 individual equities (NVDA, MSFT, AAPL, etc.) using premarket signals. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), and the paper's central claim requires cross-sectional evaluation across multiple stocks to validate the hybrid neural-classical framework's generalization. A single futures contract cannot substitute for the equity cross-section the paper depends on.
2608.08825v1.title: Hybrid Neural-Classical Correction for Frozen Time Series Foundation Models: A Comprehensive Ablation Study on High-Frequency Stock Prediction

2608.09188v1.claim: Closed-window equity-perpetual marks are observationally equivalent across infinitely many oracle topologies (external anchoring vs. self/peer-reference networks) unless venues disclose their adjustment rules and support restrictions, which can be tested only against cash-market reopens that break the equivalence class.
2608.09188v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies crypto equity-perpetual oracle mark formation during cash-market closures, requiring cross-venue oracle data, disclosed venue rules, and cash-market reopens for validation. We have only one futures instrument (NQ) with no access to crypto perpetual marks, venue oracle rules, or the cross-venue network structure the paper's entire identification strategy depends on.
2608.09188v1.title: When Cross-Venue Agreement Is Not Price Discovery: Disclosure Frontiers for 24/7 Equity-Perpetual Oracles

2608.09378v1.claim: Stablecoin transaction value distributions on Ethereum exhibit two distinct power-law scaling regimes: EOA-involved transactions cluster around exponent 1.45–1.60, while SC-SC transactions exhibit higher exponents of 1.72–1.73, with this separation robust across periods and stablecoins.
2608.09378v1.feasibility_reason: This paper analyzes blockchain transaction data (USDT/USDC on Ethereum) to estimate power-law exponents in stablecoin transfer value distributions. We have only NQ futures tick data with no blockchain, token, or cross-asset information. The paper's core claim—that transaction value distributions exhibit interaction-specific scaling regimes depending on whether transfers involve EOAs or smart contracts—requires blockchain transaction-level data that we do not possess.
2608.09378v1.title: Scaling laws of Stablecoin Transactions: Evidence from USDT and USDC on the Ethereum blockchain

2608.09641v1.claim: The smallest eigenvalues of financial correlation matrices contain information about market synchronization and effective dimensionality reduction, with predictive power for systemic risk that exceeds upper-spectrum indicators.
2608.09641v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a cross-sectional correlation matrix of multiple assets to compute eigenvalue spectra and apply Random Matrix Theory. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), so no correlation structure exists. The methodology fundamentally depends on analyzing how eigenvalues of an N×N correlation matrix behave across assets—this requires N > 1 assets observed simultaneously.
2608.09641v1.title: Lower spectrum of financial correlation matrices: a new perspective on market synchronization

2608.10693v1.claim: Machine learning models (ConvLSTM) can forecast the implied volatility surface of S&P 500 index options and capture pre-FOMC announcement effects better than a random walk benchmark.
2608.10693v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires an implied volatility surface constructed from options on S&P 500 index. We have only NQ futures tick data with no options, no quotes, no bid/ask, and no option prices. An IV surface cannot be constructed from futures alone.
2608.10693v1.title: When the Fed Speaks: Dynamics and Forecasts of the Volatility Surface

2608.10788v1.claim: The Triadic Stress Index, built from closed triangles and network properties of asset correlation matrices, detects systemic financial stress as well as or better than spectral baselines like the Absorption Ratio, while providing parameter-free per-asset attribution of stress concentration.
2608.10788v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests a network-based systemic stress index on correlation matrices of multiple asset classes (equities, crypto, commodities, FX, sovereign debt) across 20-year histories with dozens to hundreds of assets per test. We have only one instrument (NQ futures) with 384 training sessions, making cross-sectional correlation networks impossible and the sample size far too small for the paper's methodology.
2608.10788v1.title: The Triadic Stress Index in Financial Markets

2608.10852v2.adaptation: Test whether NQ futures alone exhibits the ordinal and visibility-graph properties the paper attributes to equity markets (CECP coordinates, high-degree DHVG asymmetry). This becomes a single-instrument characterization study rather than a crypto–equity comparison. The claim shifts from 'cryptocurrencies differ from equities' to 'NQ exhibits these specific ordinal and visibility signatures.' The paper's comparative structure and its conclusion about asset-class heterogeneity cannot be preserved.
2608.10852v2.claim: Cryptocurrencies and equity-index futures share heavy-tailed distributions and volatility clustering but differ in local ordinal organization (weaker for crypto) and high-degree visibility asymmetry (larger for crypto), detectable via CECP and DHVG diagnostics at one-minute resolution.
2608.10852v2.feasibility_reason: The paper's core claim—that cryptocurrencies and equity futures share macroscopic stylized facts but differ in ordinal structure and time-directed visibility—can be tested on NQ futures tick data. However, the paper compares three cryptocurrencies against one equity benchmark (S&P 500 futures). We have only NQ futures, eliminating the cross-asset comparison that is central to the paper's design.
2608.10852v2.gate_reason: The paper offers no acceptance protocol, null construction, multiple-testing correction, or measurement of out-of-sample decay. Its diagnostics (CECP, DHVG) are applied post-hoc to characterize data, not to evaluate a predictive claim or establish significance thresholds. It does not bear on how we judge a result.
2608.10852v2.relevance_reason: The paper characterizes statistical properties of price series (ordinal organization, visibility-graph structure) but proposes no mechanism a strategy could act on and no condition under which an edge would appear. Even after Stage 1's adaptation to single-instrument characterization, it remains a descriptive study of market microstructure with no actionable claim.
2608.10852v2.title: Universality and Heterogeneity of Stylized Facts in Cryptocurrency and Equity Markets

2608.11250v1.claim: An autonomous alpha-discovery system combining LLM proposal, adversarial verification, and pending-aware budget allocation can produce platform-validated trading factors with Fitness and Sharpe metrics comparable to or exceeding published benchmarks.
2608.11250v1.feasibility_reason: AgonAlpha discovers cross-sectional equity alphas on WorldQuant BRAIN using fundamental, technical, and options data across a broad universe (U.S. TOP3000). We have only one futures contract (NQ) with tick-level trade data, no cross-section, no fundamentals, no options, and no multi-asset universe. The paper's central claim—that an LLM-driven system can autonomously discover and verify trading factors—requires the ability to test factors across many securities and data types that we do not have.
2608.11250v1.title: AgonAlpha: Autonomous Alpha Discovery via Prompt Economy and Scalable Agentic Search

2608.11327v1.claim: A transformer trained on sparse sets of (account, quarter, value) tuples outperforms classical ML, chained gradient boosting, LLMs, and foundation models at forecasting complete financial statements 1–20 quarters ahead.
2608.11327v1.feasibility_reason: The paper forecasts complete financial statements (78 accounting line items) 1–20 quarters ahead using quarterly Compustat data. We have only one futures instrument (NQ) with tick-level trade data, no financial statements, no accounting items, and no fundamental data whatsoever. The paper's entire task—predicting balance sheets, income statements, and cash flows—is structurally impossible on intraday futures prices.
2608.11327v1.title: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Complete Financial Statements with Forma

2608.11505v1.claim: A well-specified Dixon-Coles structural model of match outcomes carries zero incremental information beyond de-vigged bookmaker closing prices, as measured by logarithmic opinion pool weight.
2608.11505v1.feasibility_reason: This paper tests whether a structural forecasting model adds information beyond bookmaker closing prices in association football. It requires (1) match-level outcomes with associated betting odds, (2) a cross-sectional dataset of independent events to estimate pooling weights and calibration, and (3) a domain (sports betting) entirely outside futures markets. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), no betting market data, no match outcomes, and no cross-sectional structure analogous to independent matches.
2608.11505v1.title: Does a Structural Model Add Anything to the Closing Price? Calibrated forecasting, incremental information, and match leverage in the Italian Serie A

2608.12251v1.claim: A regime-gated residual mixture-of-experts architecture improves cross-sectional volatility forecasting by using regime variables only for expert routing rather than as direct forecasting inputs.
2608.12251v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies cross-sectional volatility forecasting across 1,027 U.S. equities and 1,552 Japanese equities. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), so we cannot construct a cross-section. The entire experimental design—pooling stock-level features, computing cross-sectional correlations (IC), and evaluating on 1.9 million stock-day forecasts—requires multiple assets. A single futures contract has no cross-section.
2608.12251v1.title: Regime-Gated Residual Mixture-of-Experts for Cross-Sectional Volatility Forecasting

2608.12259v1.claim: Activation calibration strategy (abs-max vs. percentile) is a first-order determinant of 4-bit post-training quantization performance in financial time-series forecasting, with percentile calibration recovering 53–94% of degradation in affected architectures.
2608.12259v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies cross-sectional volatility forecasting on S&P 500 equities (501 stocks, daily bars, 2.1M asset-days). We have only one instrument (NQ futures) with no cross-section, no equity constituents, and no ability to construct the cross-sectional ranking task that is central to the claim. The paper's metric (daily information coefficient from cross-sectional Spearman correlation) requires multiple assets ranked on the same date.
2608.12259v1.title: Calibration Bets on the Past: Post-Training Quantization for Financial Time-Series Forecasting

2608.12424v2.claim: A Bayesian vector autoregression model integrating topic analysis, sentiment analysis, and macroeconomic variables can forecast interest rate swap curves more accurately than traditional econometric models, improving strategic asset-liability management in banks.
2608.12424v2.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim is that an AI-driven multiscenario interest rate forecasting system improves banking ALM and risk management. This requires monthly macroeconomic data (inflation, industrial production, PMI, ECB rates, commodity prices, equity indices) and interest rate swap curves across multiple maturities (2Y, 5Y, 10Y, 30Y). Our data is intraday NQ futures tick data with no macroeconomic variables, no interest rates, no cross-asset data, and no monthly aggregation capability that would preserve the economic relationships the paper models.
2608.12424v2.title: AI-Driven Multiscenario Interest Rate Forecasting: A Proof of Concept for Banking Asset Management

2608.12493v1.claim: Implied variance surfaces evolve under spot movements according to a transport velocity field whose jets govern level, skew, and curvature dynamics, and this field can be nonparametrically identified from market data and tested against classical stickiness regimes.
2608.12493v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a cross-sectional implied volatility surface (multiple strikes and maturities) to estimate transport coefficients and test smile dynamics. We have only one instrument (NQ futures) with no options data, no implied volatility surface, and no quotes or order-book depth. The empirical work (Section 8) uses five years of SPX implied-volatility snapshots across seven tenors and eleven moneyness levels—data we cannot construct from futures tick data.
2608.12493v1.title: Beyond the Skew-Stickiness Ratio: Transport Geometry of Spot-Driven Variance Surface Dynamics

2608.12583v1.claim: Diffusion generative models are effective tools for modeling complex financial data across time series, limit order books, tabular records, and structured financial objects.
2608.12583v1.feasibility_reason: This is a survey paper reviewing diffusion-model applications across financial data types (time series, limit order books, tabular data, structured objects). It makes no testable empirical claim about market behavior or trading performance. The paper's value is organizational and methodological—cataloging existing work—not predictive or causal. Testing it would require implementing dozens of distinct models on different data modalities, which is outside the scope of validating a single claim.
2608.12583v1.title: Diffusion Models in Finance: A Survey

2608.12594v1.claim: A CatBoost model trained on private company attributes can learn valuation-conditioned peer similarity that outperforms unsupervised distance metrics in k-NN valuation tasks.
2608.12594v1.feasibility_reason: This paper studies private company peer identification and valuation using cross-sectional company attributes (industry, geography, deal stage, financials) across ~53,000 firms. It requires a cross-sectional dataset of multiple companies with their characteristics and valuations. Our data is a single futures instrument (NQ) with intraday tick-level trade data, containing no company fundamentals, no cross-section, and no valuation targets. The paper's supervised similarity learning framework is fundamentally incompatible with univariate time-series futures data.
2608.12594v1.title: What Makes a Peer? Valuation-Anchored Similarity in Private Markets

2608.12634v1.claim: Official Shariah-compliant classification changes alter the feasible investor base sufficiently to produce measurable price effects when the affected security is sufficiently tradable, but formal eligibility alone is insufficient without institutional recognition and marginal constrained demand.
2608.12634v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a cross-section of equities with heterogeneous Shariah-screening classifications and official list events. We have only one futures instrument (NQ), which has no Shariah screening, no official classification lists, and no investor-mandate segmentation by religious compliance rules. The mechanism—institutional rules determining who may own a security and how classification changes affect segmented investor bases—is entirely absent from futures markets.
2608.12634v1.title: The Price of Permission: Classification Uncertainty in Constrained Capital Markets

2608.13082v1.claim: An embedding-based metric (LOB-ID) using DeepLOB Inception features can evaluate synthetic limit order book data by detecting joint temporal and cross-level structure that statistic-based and moment-matching approaches miss.
2608.13082v1.feasibility_reason: The paper evaluates synthetic limit order book (LOB) generative models using Level-2 order-book data with bid/ask depth across ten price levels. We have only tick-level trade data with aggressor side for a single futures contract, with no order-book depth, no quotes, and no message-level order flow. The core claim—that LOB-ID captures joint temporal and cross-level structure in Level-2 trajectories—cannot be tested without the multi-level book data that defines the paper's entire evaluation framework.
2608.13082v1.title: LOB-ID: Evaluating Synthetic Market Data by Inception Distances

2608.13096v1.claim: Flow-matching models can generate realistic multi-level limit order book continuations more efficiently than diffusion models while maintaining controllability over market regimes (trend, volatility, liquidity, imbalance).
2608.13096v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim is that a flow-matching generative model can produce realistic limit order book (LOB) trajectories with controllable scenario generation. This requires order book depth data (ten price levels per side with prices and volumes), which we do not have. We only have tick-level trade data with aggressor side, not the full LOB state at each timestamp.
2608.13096v1.title: FlowLOB: Efficient and Controllable Limit Order Book Generation with Flow Matching

2608.13732v2.claim: A numerical algorithm based on local time-space calculus can efficiently compute first-passage time distributions for diffusion processes through time-dependent barriers by reducing the problem to a regularized Volterra integral equation solved via product integration and Markov chain approximation.
2608.13732v2.feasibility_reason: This is a pure mathematics paper on numerical methods for solving Volterra integral equations arising from first-passage time problems in diffusion processes. It contains no empirical testing, no financial application, and no claim about market behavior or trading strategy performance. The paper derives theoretical algorithms and demonstrates them on synthetic examples (Bessel, CEV, Feller processes) with known closed-form solutions or controlled parameters—not market data.
2608.13732v2.title: On the First Hitting Time Problems for Diffusion Processes: Local Time-Space Approach

2608.14014v1.claim: News-aligned price moves concentrate before and at publication for most event types, with markets underreacting to quantified fundamental news and overreacting to soft narrative news, as measured by beta-adjusted abnormal returns across thousands of stock-day events.
2608.14014v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a cross-sectional study of ~3,000 US stocks with daily news events and returns measured across a large sample (1.68M events, 384 trading days). We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-sectional analysis impossible. The paper's findings depend on comparing how different stocks and news types react to events—a comparison that requires multiple securities.
2608.14014v1.title: Buy the Rumor, Sell the News: When Is News Priced In?

2608.14323v1.claim: A neural network architecture derived from the dependence structure among firm characteristics (via MFCF-induced cliques) predicts cross-sectional stock returns more accurately in ranking than a hand-tuned three-layer network, using 80× fewer parameters.
2608.14323v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a cross-section of firm characteristics (94 characteristics per stock) to estimate dependence structure and predict relative returns across many stocks. We have only one instrument (NQ futures) with no firm-level data, characteristics, or cross-sectional dimension. The method is fundamentally designed for equity cross-sections, not single-instrument time series.
2608.14323v1.title: Dependence-Informed Sparse Neural Architecture for Stock Return Prediction

2608.14859v1.claim: Disclosed human-capital disruption in earnings calls predicts firm-specific idiosyncratic volatility, downside risk, and executive turnover within firms over time.
2608.14859v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires cross-sectional equity data (13,201 firm-years across 2,870 firms with earnings calls, accounting data, and executive rosters). We have only one futures instrument (NQ) with 384 training sessions, making cross-sectional analysis and firm-level variation impossible. The paper measures firm-specific risk and organizational outcomes; neither construct applies to a single commodity futures contract.
2608.14859v1.title: Disclosed Human-Capital Disruption and Firm-Specific Risk

2608.15597v1.claim: A public-blockchain architecture can represent Indonesian carbon credits (SPE-GRK) as tokenized real-world assets while preserving authoritative registry control and enabling regulated programmable trading.
2608.15597v1.feasibility_reason: This paper proposes a blockchain architecture for tokenizing Indonesian carbon credits. It is a systems design and policy paper with no empirical claims testable on financial market data. It requires carbon registry data (SRUK), regulatory frameworks, and institutional coordination—none of which exist in our NQ futures dataset.
2608.15597v1.title: Toward Decentralized Carbon Trading in Indonesia: A Public-Blockchain Architecture for Tokenized Real-World Assets

2608.15640v1.claim: Under certain detectability thresholds and validator power distributions (whales and minnows), large validators (whales) suffer reduced expected profits from joining a censorship attack, deterring their participation and preventing the attack's success.
2608.15640v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is a theoretical game-theoretic analysis of blockchain validator incentives and censorship attacks. It requires modeling validator behavior, stake distributions, and consensus protocol mechanics—none of which exist in single-instrument futures data. The claim concerns blockchain economics, not price prediction or trading.
2608.15640v1.title: A contribution to the critique of blockchain censorship

2608.15841v1.claim: Automatically discovered auxiliary tasks (General Value Functions) improve reinforcement learning stability and profitability in multi-stock portfolio trading compared to hand-crafted auxiliary tasks and baseline RL methods.
2608.15841v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests a multi-stock portfolio trading strategy on daily bars across four equity indices (DJI, FTSE, Sensex, TAIEX), each with 30 stocks. We have only 384 training sessions (daily bars), which is insufficient for the paper's cross-sectional portfolio optimization claim. The method requires learning separate auxiliary tasks and policies across multiple assets and regimes; this is a fundamentally different problem from single-instrument intraday trading on NQ futures.
2608.15841v1.title: Self-Supervised Auxiliary Task Discovery for Stable Reinforcement Learning in Stock Trading

2608.17636v1.claim: A tensor-train compressed COS method can efficiently price European multi-asset options by sampling the joint characteristic function on a frequency grid, compressing it in tensor-train format, and converting to COS coefficients for fast reuse across strikes and payoffs.
2608.17636v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is a numerical methods paper for multi-asset European option pricing under characteristic-function models. It requires access to joint characteristic functions of multiple assets and prices multi-asset derivatives (baskets, min/max options). We have only one instrument (NQ futures), no cross-sectional data, no options market, and no ability to construct multi-asset characteristic functions.
2608.17636v1.title: COS-TT-CHF: A Tensor-Train Characteristic-Function COS Method for Multi-Asset Option Pricing

2608.17808v3.claim: Self-consistent adjoint policy iteration for constrained continuous-time portfolio choice with predictable returns converges globally when the adjoint-based operator satisfies directional improvement and asymptotic stationarity compatibility conditions.
2608.17808v3.feasibility_reason: This paper develops continuous-time stochastic control theory for dynamic portfolio optimization with predictable returns and convex constraints. It requires solving fixed-policy Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations, estimating factor-dependent hedging fields via adjoints, and comparing population-level operators—all in a multi-factor, multi-asset setting. Our data is a single futures instrument with tick-level trade data, no factors, no cross-sectional dimension, and only 384 daily sessions. The paper's central claim (that self-consistent adjoint policy iteration converges globally for constrained CRRA portfolios under directional improvement conditions) cannot be tested because we lack the factor structure, multi-asset universe, and continuous-time framework the theory requires.
2608.17808v3.title: Self-Consistent Adjoint Policy Iteration for Constrained Dynamic Portfolio Choice

2608.18195v1.claim: A reinforcement learning algorithm using logistic-normal distributions and deep-set encoders can learn to maximize market-making revenue by dynamically placing limit orders across multiple price levels while managing inventory, outperforming fixed heuristic benchmarks in simulated limit-order-book environments with noise, tactical, and strategic traders.
2608.18195v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires testing a market-making RL algorithm in a simulated limit order book with multi-level order placement, queue positions, and adaptive responses to order-book state. We have only tick-level NQ futures data with aggressor side, no order-book depth, no queue positions, no ability to inject fills or simulate counterparty responses. The paper explicitly states it uses 'stochastic market simulators that organically interact with the RL agent'—we cannot construct this interaction on real trade data without fabricating order fills and book state.
2608.18195v1.title: Multi-Level Market Making with Reinforcement Learning

2608.22768v1.title: The Loop-Gain Matrix: Coupled Rebalancing Feedback and the Blind Spots of Scalar Stability Monitoring
