2609.00438v1.title: Single- and Multilevel Quadrature with Error Control for Fourier Pricing under the Rough Heston Model

2609.00731v1.claim: LLM agents can autonomously discover novel, non-redundant, out-of-sample-valid cross-sectional equity factors that outperform baseline discovery systems when evaluated on multiple axes (productivity, performance, novelty) and re-executed across historical decision dates.
2609.00731v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim concerns autonomous LLM-based discovery of cross-sectional equity factors on panels of 400+ characteristics. We have one futures contract with ~87 derived features at best, no cross-section of assets to rank within each period, and no characteristic panel. Factor discovery requires ranking stocks monthly by a formula; NQ futures has no stock universe.
2609.00731v1.title: Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing: Methodological Foundations

2609.01323v1.claim: An adaptive singular-point dynamic-programming method can efficiently price and hedge surrenderable equity-linked insurance contracts under correlated stochastic volatility and interest rates while controlling representation error and achieving Delta consistency.
2609.01323v1.feasibility_reason: This paper develops a deterministic numerical method for pricing and hedging long-dated equity-linked life-insurance contracts with stochastic volatility, stochastic interest rates, mortality, and Bermudan surrender options. It requires mortality tables, insurance contract specifications (guarantees, surrender payoffs, premium schedules), and a term structure of interest rates—none of which exist in our data. The core claim concerns insurance liability valuation under multiple stochastic factors and optimal exercise, not trading strategy or market microstructure.
2609.01323v1.title: Adaptive singular-point method for pricing and hedging surrenderable equity-linked contracts

2609.02014v1.claim: Time-consistent dynamic CVaR hedging via elicitable risk measures and actor-critic RL produces superior risk control over shorter horizons compared to static (precommitment) CVaR hedging, with performance depending on the choice of strictly consistent scoring function.
2609.02014v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies dynamic hedging of a European basket option on four bank stocks using deep reinforcement learning with time-consistent CVaR risk measures. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), no cross-sectional data, no options, no implied volatility, and no ability to construct a basket or multi-asset portfolio. The core claim requires multiple underlyings, option pricing, and portfolio construction—none of which are available.
2609.02014v1.title: Insights on Time-consistent Deep Hedging under Elicitable Dynamic Risk Measures

2609.02447v1.claim: The order of composition between a nonlinear instantaneous impact law and a memory kernel determines whether price manipulation is possible: nonlinearity before memory forces affinity, while nonlinearity after memory requires complete positivity of the kernel.
2609.02447v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is a pure mathematical treatment of transient market impact models and price manipulation in abstract settings. It requires testing on multiple instruments with cross-sectional variation, or at minimum requires the ability to estimate and validate the nonlinear impact functions and memory kernels it theorizes about. We have one futures contract with no ability to separate impact law from memory kernel empirically, and no way to construct the round-trip cost tests the paper's theorems demand across different market regimes or instruments.
2609.02447v1.title: Price manipulation in nonlinear transient impact models: rigidity before memory and complete positivity after memory

2609.02660v1.adaptation: Test the GA-ACD model's ability to capture any duration clustering in NQ futures (if present), or test it on simulated data with artificial heaping. The core claim about FX heaping cannot be adapted—it is a market-specific phenomenon absent from futures markets.
2609.02660v1.claim: A mixture-distribution ACD model accounting for integer-second heaping in trade durations provides better fit and unbiased parameter estimates than standard ACD models when heaping is present.
2609.02660v1.feasibility_reason: The paper models trade duration distributions and dynamics in FX markets using tick-level data. We have tick-level NQ futures data with aggressor side, which allows duration modeling. However, the paper's empirical claim about FX-specific heaping (integer-second clustering from data reporting conventions) cannot be tested on NQ futures—this phenomenon is documented as specific to FX markets and absent in stock/equity futures markets. The methodological contribution (GA-ACD model) is testable, but the empirical phenomenon it addresses is not present in our data.
2609.02660v1.gate_reason: The paper offers no acceptance protocol, null construction, overfitting method, or measurement of out-of-sample decay that would inform how we judge a result. It is a model-fitting contribution, not an evaluation contribution.
2609.02660v1.relevance_reason: The paper's contribution is a duration model (GA-ACD) with no edge claim a strategy could act on. Stage 1 correctly identified that integer-second heaping is absent from NQ futures, removing the empirical phenomenon the model was designed to capture. What remains—a better-fitting duration distribution—is a measurement improvement with no actionable consequence for trading.
2609.02660v1.title: Modeling Trade Durations under Temporal Granularity Effects in Forex Markets

2609.03115v1.claim: Heterogeneous agents trading on forecasts over different horizons generate equilibrium prices whose local regularity depends on whether the rough predictable signal is cancelled by market impact, with cancellation requiring agents' horizon distribution to satisfy specific conditions.
2609.03115v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is a theoretical mean-field equilibrium model of heterogeneous agents' trading behavior under market impact. It requires testing predictions about how aggregate positions, forecast horizons, and price components interact—none of which can be observed or constructed from single-instrument tick data. The model's central claims concern equilibrium kernels, signal cancellation conditions, and Hölder regularity of prices under specific horizon distributions; these are properties of the theoretical equilibrium, not empirical predictions testable against realized price paths.
2609.03115v1.title: Mean-field equilibrium of heterogeneous agents under market impact

2609.03552v1.claim: An entropy-minimization framework for portfolio replication produces lower turnover and superior net returns compared to OLS, especially during market stress, by acting as a probabilistic circuit breaker that reduces exposure to structurally uncertain assets.
2609.03552v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires replicating a target benchmark (S&P 500, SPY, or a hybrid portfolio) using a basket of constituent assets. This is fundamentally a cross-sectional problem: it needs multiple assets with correlated returns to construct a replicating portfolio. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), so there is no basket of assets to combine, no cross-asset correlation structure to exploit, and no portfolio weights to optimize across constituents.
2609.03552v1.title: An Entropic Factor Model for Robust Portfolio Replication

2609.04087v1.claim: A global framework for joint S&P 500–VIX smile calibration across multiple maturities can be formulated without Markovian conditional-independence restrictions, and the stitched model is a strict subset of globally feasible path laws that discards cross-period dependence relevant to multi-period pricing.
2609.04087v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim concerns joint SPX–VIX smile calibration across multiple maturities using options data (SPX and VIX option prices, implied volatilities, bid–ask surfaces). We have only one futures instrument (NQ) with tick-level trade data, no options, no implied volatility surfaces, no bid–ask quotes, and no VIX data. The entire mathematical framework (martingale optimal transport, dispersion constraints, smile calibration, option-price moments) requires options market data that we do not possess.
2609.04087v1.title: Global Multi-Maturity SPX-VIX Calibration Beyond Markovian Stitching

2609.04420v1.claim: Optimal stratified allocation for rare-event subset construction is equal (not proportional) class counts under class-weighted loss, and this allocation dominates uniform and proportional designs in finite-population variance and empirical forecasting performance.
2609.04420v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim concerns optimal stratified allocation for rare-event forecasting in dependent sequences, tested on 350 U.S. equities over 2004–2011 with five forward test periods. We have one instrument (NQ futures) with 384 train, 86 validation, 73 holdout sessions—a cross-sectional constraint of ~460 total observations. The paper requires a cross-sectional panel of many securities to test allocation theory; a single futures contract cannot supply the multi-security structure needed.
2609.04420v1.title: Optimal Stratified Allocation for Rare-Event Onset Forecasting in Dependent Sequences

2609.04569v1.claim: A single-qubit parameterized quantum circuit can approximate Bitcoin realized volatility and generate synthetic time series that reproduce empirical multifractal properties including anti-persistence in volatility increments (Hurst exponent ~0.05-0.1) and near-random return dynamics (Hurst exponent ~0.5).
2609.04569v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires Bitcoin realized volatility (RV) constructed from 5-minute intraday price data, which we do not have. We have only NQ futures tick data with no Bitcoin prices. Additionally, the paper's analysis is fundamentally about Bitcoin volatility dynamics and multifractal properties specific to that asset; testing on NQ futures would be testing a different claim entirely.
2609.04569v1.title: Quantum Circuit Learning for Volatility Modeling: Multifractal Analysis of Realized Volatility Time Series

2609.04712v1.claim: A convex quadratic model of transient cross-impact cost, coupling trades across related contracts via a positive semidefinite matrix and across time via power-law decay, improves relative-value trading by correctly pricing the partial cancellation of correlated legs' impacts.
2609.04712v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires modeling cross-impact between multiple related contracts (nearby and deferred WTI futures) and testing relative-value spread trading. We have only one instrument (NQ front month), so cross-impact cannot be observed or tested. The claim is fundamentally about multi-contract portfolio construction and cannot be adapted to a single-contract setting.
2609.04712v1.title: Convex Modeling of Price Cross-Impact over Time

2609.04917v1.claim: Within the public evidence examined through August 2026, no general AI architecture is shown to deliver persistent, cross-regime, capacity-aware net alpha across equities, crypto spot, perpetual futures, and on-chain markets.
2609.04917v1.feasibility_reason: This is a critical literature review of AI profitability claims across equities, ETFs, crypto spot, perpetual futures, and on-chain markets. It requires a cross-sectional, multi-asset, multi-timeframe evidence base with fundamentals, news, sentiment, on-chain data, and comparative benchmarks. We have one futures instrument with tick data only.
2609.04917v1.title: Artificial Intelligence in Equity and Crypto Markets: Progress, Profitability Evidence, and the Limits of Automated Investing

2609.05491v1.claim: Neural networks with asymptotic-regime-aware architectures can compute Black-Scholes implied volatility from option prices more accurately than standard feed-forward networks.
2609.05491v1.feasibility_reason: This paper solves a pure numerical problem: inverting the Black-Scholes formula to compute implied volatility from option prices. It requires options data (prices, strikes, maturities, rates) as inputs. We have only NQ futures tick data with no options, no option prices, no strikes, no maturities—the entire input domain of the paper does not exist in our dataset.
2609.05491v1.title: Asymptotically-informed neural networks for Black-Scholes implied volatility computation

2609.06085v1.acts_on: A strategy would condition flow-continuation predictions on whether the previous return was zero vs. non-zero, and would model signed-volume impact as saturating rather than linear. This is a concrete edit to the state space.
2609.06085v1.adaptation: Test on intraday NQ futures (1-minute or 5-minute bars) rather than daily bars. This preserves the high-frequency price-volume dynamics the paper studies. Daily bars (384 sessions) are infeasible for the statistical power needed to estimate and validate the nonlinear parametric model and its Shapley decomposition.
2609.06085v1.claim: Neural networks trained on lagged returns and signed volumes learn interpretable nonlinear price-impact and order-flow-persistence mechanisms that can be extracted via Shapley decomposition and encoded in a parsimonious parametric model competitive with the neural network itself.
2609.06085v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies intraday price-volume dynamics using neural networks and explainability on NASDAQ stocks. We have NQ futures tick data with buy/sell volume, which is structurally similar. However, the paper uses 10 stocks (5 large-tick, 5 small-tick) from June 2024 with ~50% train/test split, yielding roughly 200k+ intraday observations per stock. Our constraint is 384 training sessions (daily bars), which is ~1,800× fewer observations. The claim is testable on intraday NQ bars, but not on daily bars—sample size is the binding constraint.
2609.06085v1.gate_reason: The paper offers no acceptance protocol, null construction, overfitting correction, or measurement of out-of-sample decay that would change how we judge a result. Its contribution is a mechanism (nonlinear saturation) and a method (Shapley decomposition) to extract it; neither bears on the gate's error rates, thresholds, or falsified-families list.
2609.06085v1.hypothesis_edit: Add to intraday-continuation: split the continuation/reversal prediction by lagged-return sign and magnitude; test whether nonlinear (saturating) signed-volume impact outperforms linear volume in predicting next-bar direction.
2609.06085v1.relevance_reason: The paper's separable claim—that lagged signed volume generates nonlinear, saturating price-impact effects and that lagged returns act as state variables conditioning flow persistence—is testable on intraday NQ and could refine the continuation/reversal question. However, it does not directly address an open hypothesis; it would add a state-conditioning mechanism to questions already closed (intraday-continuation rejected 6 times), and the mechanism itself (nonlinear saturation in volume impact) was not the binding constraint in those rejections.
2609.06085v1.speaks_to_deferral: None. The paper does not address a deferred question (regime models, RL, deep networks). It proposes a mechanism for a closed question.
2609.06085v1.title: Explainable Deep Learning for Price-Trade Dynamics: From Black-Box Forecasts to Effective Parametric Models

2609.06137v1.claim: A correction formula can restore unbiased Greeks for discontinuous payoffs by decomposing sensitivity into a pathwise term plus boundary corrections, without requiring smoothing or per-product calibration.
2609.06137v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is about computing unbiased sensitivities (Greeks) for exotic derivatives with discontinuous payoffs using Monte Carlo simulation and automatic differentiation. It requires the ability to price and differentiate complex structured products (barriers, autocallables, digitals) with recursive logic and multiple indicators. Our data is a single futures contract with only trade-level tick data; we have no ability to define, price, or compute Greeks for any derivative payoff structure, nor do we have the pricing models (GBM, Heston, Hull-White) or AAD infrastructure the paper depends on.
2609.06137v1.title: Unbiased Monte Carlo Greeks for Discontinuous Payoffs

2609.06267v1.claim: Return-to-Present curves provide a superior graphical representation for comparing realized historical performance of multiple investments by fixing an evaluation endpoint and varying historical purchase dates, making entry-date sensitivity, relative dominance, and performance crossings directly visible.
2609.06267v1.feasibility_reason: This paper proposes a visualization method for comparing historical returns across different entry dates to a fixed endpoint. It requires multiple comparable investment price series (stocks, ETFs, funds) to demonstrate its utility. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making peer comparisons, sector comparisons, and multi-asset allocation examples—the paper's core use cases—impossible to construct.
2609.06267v1.title: From Discrete Trailing Returns to a Continuous Graphical Profile: Return-to-Present Curves

2609.06422v1.adaptation: Estimate ALM-GARCH on daily NQ futures returns instead of the six equity indices and Bitcoin. The model mechanics and statistical tests remain unchanged, but the claim shifts from 'asymmetry channels are pervasive across international equities and crypto' to 'asymmetry channels are present in NQ futures.' The paper's main finding—that the level channel is rejected everywhere while the memory channel is selective—can be tested, but only on one instrument rather than six.
2609.06422v1.claim: Positive and negative return innovations enter conditional variance with different amplitudes (level channel) and kernel offsets (memory channel), and these two channels can be separately identified and tested via likelihood-ratio tests in a finite-dimensional Markov model.
2609.06422v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests a volatility model (ALM-GARCH) on daily equity index and Bitcoin returns. We have NQ futures tick data from which we can construct daily bars, giving us 384 train sessions—sufficient for a daily volatility study. However, the paper's empirical claims rest on testing across six different assets (five equity indices plus Bitcoin) to establish generality of the asymmetry channels. Testing on a single instrument (NQ) changes the scope from a cross-asset validation to a single-asset case study.
2609.06422v1.gate_reason: The paper contributes nothing to acceptance protocols, multiple-testing corrections, null constructions, out-of-sample decay measurement, or falsified-family documentation. Its out-of-sample performance is 'broadly comparable to standard benchmarks'—a null result on volatility forecasting that does not change how we judge a trading result, and does not contradict or refine any gate criterion.
2609.06422v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a volatility model with no edge to trade. It estimates parameters, tests statistical hypotheses about variance dynamics, and reports out-of-sample performance 'broadly comparable to standard benchmarks'—which means no actionable claim survives removal of the apparatus. A strategy cannot act on 'the level channel is rejected' or 'memory channel is weakly identified for KOSPI'; these are model diagnostics, not trading signals.
2609.06422v1.title: Asymmetric Long-Memory GARCH: Sign-Dependent Kernel Injection in a Two-Dimensional Markov Chain

2609.07207v1.adaptation: Test the claim on intraday NQ bars (1-minute, 5-minute, or 10-minute) rather than trade-by-trade data. The robust filtering methodology applies directly to any price series, but the paper's specific finding about microstructure noise variance being infinite and the resulting flat volatility signature at the 1-second level is an equity-specific empirical claim. On NQ futures, test whether robust (Huber) filtering produces flatter volatility signatures than linear filtering at available intraday resolutions, accepting that the noise structure and optimal filter parameters will differ from equities.
2609.07207v1.claim: Robust (Huber-loss) filtering of prices produces flatter volatility signature plots (invariant to aggregation interval) compared to linear filtering, because it resists heavy-tailed microstructure noise.
2609.07207v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's core claim—that robust filtering (Huber loss) produces flatter volatility signatures than linear filtering on high-frequency trade data—can be tested on NQ futures. However, the paper's empirical validation relies on 1.5M trades per day from a single stock (NVDA), whereas NQ futures have different microstructure. The binding constraint is sample size: we have only 384 training sessions (days), which is sufficient for daily volatility signature analysis, but the paper's detailed intraday findings (1-second, 10-second returns) depend on within-day trade structure that may differ materially between equities and futures.
2609.07207v1.gate_reason: The paper's methodology — a robust filtering approach that resists heavy-tailed noise — bears on how we measure the state variables we condition on. If volatility estimates are biased by microstructure noise at intraday resolutions, that affects the reliability of any volatility-based gate or state measurement in our protocol. The flat signature claim, if true on NQ, would validate that robust filtering removes a known source of measurement error.
2609.07207v1.protocol_edit: If robust filtering produces materially different volatility estimates than linear methods on NQ intraday bars, add a note to the gate's state-measurement section: volatility conditioning should use Huber-loss filtering rather than linear methods to avoid microstructure-noise bias. This is a measurement refinement, not a new hypothesis.
2609.07207v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a measurement technique (robust filtering for volatility estimation) with no edge to trade on. It answers 'how do we measure volatility better' but not 'what should a strategy do differently'. The adapted claim about flat volatility signatures is a stylised fact about noise, not a condition under which returns are predictable or a mechanism a strategy acts on.
2609.07207v1.title: Filtering without recursion and some of its uses in financial economics

2609.07989v1.adaptation: Replace NASDAQ equity order flow with NQ E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures order flow. Aggregate signed volume into buckets (volume-clock or time-clock) to create univariate signed-volume series. The univariate BOCPD vs. BOSD comparison (Section 7) is directly testable; the multivariate BOCPDMS experiments (Section 12) are infeasible without a second instrument. The paper's claim about log-normal duration laws fitting order flow better than geometric or Pareto can be tested on futures order flow, but the result may differ due to different market microstructure (futures vs. equities, different participant composition, different order-splitting behavior).
2609.07989v1.claim: Duration-aware Bayesian online changepoint detection with log-normal regime durations outperforms constant-hazard BOCPD at segmenting and forecasting order flow regimes.
2609.07989v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's core claim—that duration-aware Bayesian online changepoint detection (BOSD) outperforms constant-hazard BOCPD on order flow—can be tested on NQ futures tick data. However, the paper uses NASDAQ equity order flow (AAPL, MSFT) aggregated into volume-clock buckets. Testing requires adapting to intraday NQ futures order flow at tick or bar resolution, which changes the microstructure properties being studied.
2609.07989v1.gate_reason: The paper's protocol for evaluating changepoint detection (likelihood, forecasting accuracy, regime duration fit) is methodologically sound and could inform how we measure regime stability if that question is reopened. However, it does not directly constrain or improve the current gate, which is built for single-regime hypothesis testing.
2609.07989v1.protocol_edit: If regime detection is deferred to a later phase, document this paper's acceptance criteria (log-likelihood improvement threshold, out-of-sample forecast accuracy metric, duration-law fit test) as a reference protocol for that phase. It establishes a baseline for what 'better regime detection' means and how to measure it.
2609.07989v1.relevance_reason: The paper proposes a regime-detection method, but the project explicitly defers regime models as a later and harder question. The claim is inseparable from the apparatus (BOCPD variants), and nothing actionable survives its removal—no features, mechanism, or condition a strategy could act on without the fitted changepoint detector.
2609.07989v1.speaks_to_deferral: Not a regime model. If flow continues in some conditions and reverses in others, that is a later and harder question.
2609.07989v1.title: Regimes in the Order Flow

2609.08060v1.claim: A minimal one-stage logistic paired-comparison model with exponentially-weighted team form and ridge-shrunk strengths forecasts professional League of Legends match outcomes as accurately as a more complex two-stage mixed model, and matches prediction market pricing.
2609.08060v1.feasibility_reason: This paper models esports match outcomes using paired-comparison methods on a cross-sectional dataset of 5,135 games. It requires esports match data (League of Legends), team rosters, draft information, and prediction market prices—none of which exist in our NQ futures dataset. The core claim (that a one-stage logistic model matches a two-stage mixed model for win prediction) is entirely domain-specific and cannot be adapted to single-instrument financial data.
2609.08060v1.title: Pre-game paired-comparison modeling of professional League of Legends map outcomes

2609.08106v1.claim: Nyström low-rank attention (m=32 landmarks) matches full O(N²) cross-sectional stock attention at O(mN) cost while sparsification fails, because the deviation from uniformity in learned attention is low-rank and dynamic.
2609.08106v1.feasibility_reason: The paper studies cross-sectional stock prediction using multi-stock attention mechanisms on a universe of 300–3,486 stocks. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), making cross-sectional analysis impossible. The core claim—that Nyström attention approximates full cross-stock attention—requires a stock universe; it cannot be tested on a single futures contract.
2609.08106v1.title: Nyström Attention Matches Full Attention for Cross-Sectional Stock Prediction

2609.08581v1.claim: AlphaRJM discovers interpretable formulaic alphas by combining persistent reward-jump memory of terminal evaluation feedback with stochastic return-guided symbolic search, outperforming prior methods across multiple equity universes and forecasting horizons.
2609.08581v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests formulaic alpha discovery on Chinese equity cross-sections (CSI300, CSI500, CSI800) with 11 years of daily data (2010–2024), yielding thousands of daily observations per universe. We have only 384 training sessions on a single NQ futures contract, making cross-sectional alpha discovery impossible and providing far too few observations to validate the method's core claims about pool-dependent symbolic search and distributional return modeling.
2609.08581v1.title: AlphaRJM: Reward-Jump Memory for Stochastic Return-Guided Alpha Discovery

2609.08881v1.claim: Short-selling bans reduce left-tail price risk (maximum drawdown) more effectively in stocks with low institutional ownership, while widening bid-ask spreads more in stocks with high institutional ownership.
2609.08881v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests cross-sectional predictions about short-selling bans across 17 European equity markets using institutional ownership as a moderator. We have only one instrument (NQ futures), no cross-section of stocks, no institutional ownership data, and no ability to measure bid-ask spreads or construct the left-tail return metrics (maximum drawdown) that are central to the claims.
2609.08881v1.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Short-Selling Bans

2609.09405v1.claim: The Log S-fBM model reconciles rough and multifractal volatility through a unified framework parameterized by Hurst exponent H, and exhibits scale-invariant moment properties and testable statistical properties (rough vs. multifractal hypothesis) that can be derived in closed form under small intermittency approximation.
2609.09405v1.feasibility_reason: This is a pure mathematical statistics paper on the Log S-fBM stochastic volatility model. It derives theoretical properties (scaling, deviation inequalities, hypothesis tests, scale invariance) and validates them on synthetically generated data. It makes no empirical claim testable on real market data—it does not propose a trading strategy, a calibration method to be applied to observed returns, or a forecasting model. The numerical experiments use simulated paths, not market data.
2609.09405v1.title: The Log S-fBM model: Statistical analysis

2609.10407v1.claim: dexamine is a Python package that correctly parses and joins Uniswap v2/v3 event logs to execution metadata on Ethereum.
2609.10407v1.feasibility_reason: This paper is a software tool for parsing Ethereum blockchain data from Uniswap decentralized exchanges. It has no testable empirical claim about market behavior, trading strategy, or price prediction that could be evaluated on NQ futures data. The paper describes data infrastructure, not a hypothesis about markets.
2609.10407v1.title: dexamine: A Python package for Uniswap event data on Ethereum

2609.10865v1.claim: A new confidence interval for the difference between two independent binomial proportions, constructed by projecting an elliptical region onto the difference parameter, is conservative, admissible, and measurably superior to Wald intervals in coverage properties.
2609.10865v1.feasibility_reason: This paper develops statistical theory for confidence intervals on binomial proportions—a pure mathematical statistics problem with no connection to financial time series or trading. It requires no market data, price movements, volume, or any instrument whatsoever.
2609.10865v1.title: The Elliptically Optimal Confidence Interval: A Bivariate Extension of Wilson's Score Method

2609.11614v1.claim: A deep reinforcement-learning market maker augmented with Bayesian online change-point detection of directional order-flow regimes and queue-adjusted quote-exposure signals remains profitable under persistent regime-switching order flow, whereas stationarily trained agents and classical closed-form policies (GLFT) suffer large drawdowns.
2609.11614v1.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires a limit order book simulator with queue-aware execution mechanics, FIFO priority, and the ability to generate counterfactual regime-switching order flow. We have only tick-level trade data on one futures contract with no order book depth, no quotes, no queue position information, and no ability to control or stress-test the order-flow distribution. The paper explicitly states it trains and evaluates inside a 'queue-aware event-driven simulator' because historical data alone cannot map fills consistently across policies—a constraint that binds here.
2609.11614v1.title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow

2609.12227v1.claim: Seasonal trading signals from dummy-variable regression, Singular Spectrum Analysis, and robust SSA, when applied to multiple commodity futures contracts and ranked cross-sectionally, do not produce statistically robust out-of-sample outperformance relative to an equal-weight long benchmark after transaction costs.
2609.12227v1.feasibility_reason: The paper tests seasonal trading strategies on 15 commodity futures contracts over 108 monthly observations (2016–2024). Our data is a single instrument (NQ futures) with 384 training sessions, which cannot support a cross-sectional ranking strategy or a multi-contract portfolio. The paper's central claim requires comparing seasonal signals across multiple commodities and forming Top-1 long/short portfolios; this is impossible with one instrument.
2609.12227v1.title: Seasonal Trading in Commodity Futures: Evidence from Regression and Singular Spectrum Signals

2609.12793v1.claim: VertiFuseX, a hybrid LSTM with penultimate-layer vertical fusion of multi-scale temporal representations, achieves 30–54% MAPE reductions and generalizes robustly across 10 global equity indices under strict chronological out-of-sample testing.
2609.12793v1.feasibility_reason: The paper evaluates daily closing-price forecasting on 10 global equity indices over 15 years (384 train sessions). We have only 384 daily observations on one futures contract, making cross-index generalization claims untestable. The paper's central claim requires demonstrating robustness across diverse markets (S&P 500, DJIA, NASDAQ, DAX, HSI, KOSPI, etc.); we cannot construct a cross-section from a single NQ futures instrument.
2609.12793v1.title: VertiFuseX: Generalizable Financial Forecasting via Multi-Stream Temporal Fusion

2609.13402v3.claim: Diffusion models can generate dynamic implied-volatility surfaces that preserve no-arbitrage structure and improve data-driven hedging performance relative to classical and GAN-based benchmarks.
2609.13402v3.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires options data (implied volatility surfaces across strikes and maturities) to test dynamic surface generation and hedging. We have only NQ futures tick data with no options, no quotes, no order book, and no cross-sectional dimension. The hedging evaluation also requires a portfolio of options to hedge, which cannot be constructed from futures alone.
2609.13402v3.title: Diffusion models for dynamic volatility surface generation and data-driven hedging

2609.13597v2.claim: Observationally equivalent aggregate limit-order-book paths can imply economically different passive-execution outcomes depending on unobserved within-queue cancellation allocation rules (front vs. back vs. random).
2609.13597v2.feasibility_reason: The paper's central claim requires order-book depth data (L2 snapshots with 10 price levels) and synchronized L1 trade feeds to reconstruct FIFO queue histories and test execution fill sensitivity. We have only tick-level trade data with aggressor side on a single futures contract, with no order-book snapshots, no depth, and no ability to infer queue position or cancellation allocation rules.
2609.13597v2.title: Same Book, Different Fills: Partial Identification of FIFO Execution from Aggregate Order Books

2609.13715v1.claim: Long-memory of trade signs is an event-time statement about order splitting and hidden-order fragmentation, while square-root price impact is an operational-time statement about latent order-book front motion, and these are distinct mechanisms observed together only after subordination to calendar time.
2609.13715v1.feasibility_reason: The paper is a theoretical framework paper deriving mathematical relationships between event-time order-flow memory, operational-time impact, and calendar-time observables. It requires order-level data with hidden-order structure, meta-order fragmentation, and order-splitting information to test its central claims about the Lillo–Mike–Farmer renewal law and latent order-book dynamics. 2609.13715v1.title: Event-Time Order-Flow Memory, Operational-Time Impact, and Subordinated Market Observables
